title: Die Bienenkönigin
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 62. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original scans). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng/giengen, Thür/Thüre, Thiere und ward).
about: The sixty-second tale in the Grimms’ collection (KHM 62), a short and very clean instance of the kindest-brother pattern. Dummling, mocked by his two elders, spares an ant-hill, a lake full of ducks and a nest of bees; when the three of them reach a castle where the horses are stone and a little grey man sets three impossible tasks, the spared creatures come and do what no man could. Spelling follows the 1857 edition, so you will meet older forms such as giengen, geriethen, Thier, tödten and ward.

sentences.t: Zwei Königssöhne giengen einmal auf Abenteuer und geriethen in ein wildes, wüstes Leben, so daß sie gar nicht wieder nach Haus kamen.
sentences.l: Two king’s-sons went out once upon adventure and got into a wild, dissolute life, so that they did not come home again at all.
sentences.i: Two king’s sons once went out in search of adventure and fell into a wild, riotous life, so that they never came home again.
sentences.n: “auf Abenteuer gehen” = to go out adventuring, to seek one’s fortune. geriethen is the 1857 spelling of gerieten (geraten, to get into something, usually unintended). wüst here is not “desolate” but “dissolute, riotous.”

sentences.t: Der jüngste, welcher der Dummling hieß, machte sich auf und suchte seine Brüder: aber wie er sie endlich fand, verspotteten sie ihn, daß er mit seiner Einfalt sich durch die Welt schlagen wollte, und sie zwei könnten nicht durchkommen, und wären doch viel klüger.
sentences.l: The youngest, who was called the Dummling, set himself out and sought his brothers: but when he at last found them, they mocked him, that he with his simplicity wanted to beat his way through the world, and they two could not get through, and were yet much cleverer.
sentences.i: The youngest, who was called Dummling, set out and looked for his brothers; but when he found them at last they mocked him — that he with his simple wits meant to make his way through the world, while the two of them, far cleverer, could not manage it.
sentences.n: Dummling is a name and a verdict at once, built on dumm — roughly “the simpleton.” He is the youngest-and-least of the folktale, and we leave the name in German. “sich durch die Welt schlagen” is a set phrase: to fight one's way through life. könnten and wären are subjunctive — the jeer as reported.

sentences.t: Sie zogen alle drei miteinander fort und kamen an einen Ameisenhaufen.
sentences.l: They all three drew away together and came to an ant-heap.
sentences.i: The three of them travelled on together and came to an ant-hill.

sentences.t: Die zwei ältesten wollten ihn aufwühlen und sehen wie die kleinen Ameisen in der Angst herumkröchen und ihre Eier forttrügen, aber der Dummling sagte „laßt die Thiere in Frieden, ich leids nicht, daß ihr sie stört.“
sentences.l: The two eldest wanted to dig it up and see how the little ants would creep about in their fright and carry off their eggs, but the Dummling said “leave the animals in peace, I will not suffer it that you disturb them.”
sentences.i: The two eldest wanted to churn it up and watch the little ants scurry about in terror and carry off their eggs; but Dummling said: “Leave the creatures in peace — I will not have you troubling them.”
sentences.n: herumkröchen and forttrügen are subjunctive: what the brothers picture themselves watching, not what happens. leids = leide es; “ich leid es nicht” = I will not allow it. Thier is the 1857 spelling of Tier.

sentences.t: Da giengen sie weiter und kamen an einen See, auf dem schwammen viele viele Enten.
sentences.l: Then they went further and came to a lake, on which swam many many ducks.
sentences.i: Then they went on and came to a lake on which a great many ducks were swimming.

sentences.t: Die zwei Brüder wollten ein paar fangen und braten, aber der Dummling ließ es nicht zu, und sprach „laßt die Thiere in Frieden, ich leids nicht, daß ihr sie tödtet.“
sentences.l: The two brothers wanted to catch a couple and roast them, but the Dummling did not permit it, and spoke “leave the animals in peace, I will not suffer it that you kill them.”
sentences.i: The two brothers wanted to catch a few and roast them, but Dummling would not allow it, and said: “Leave the creatures in peace — I will not have you killing them.”
sentences.n: tödtet belongs to tödten, the 1857 spelling of töten (to kill).

sentences.t: Endlich kamen sie an ein Bienennest, darin war so viel Honig, daß er am Stamm herunterlief.
sentences.l: At last they came to a bees’ nest, in it was so much honey that it ran down the trunk.
sentences.i: At last they came to a bees’ nest with so much honey in it that it ran down the trunk of the tree.
sentences.n: darin = “therein, in it.”

sentences.t: Die zwei wollten Feuer unter den Baum legen und die Bienen ersticken, damit sie den Honig wegnehmen könnten.
sentences.l: The two wanted to lay fire under the tree and smother the bees, so that they could take the honey away.
sentences.i: The two of them wanted to set a fire under the tree and smoke the bees to death, so that they could carry off the honey.

sentences.t: Der Dummling hielt sie aber wieder ab, und sprach „laßt die Thiere in Frieden, ich leids nicht, daß ihr sie verbrennt.“
sentences.l: The Dummling however held them back again, and spoke “leave the animals in peace, I will not suffer it that you burn them.”
sentences.i: But Dummling held them back once more, and said: “Leave the creatures in peace — I will not have you burning them.”
sentences.n: The same words a third time — three creatures spared, and three tasks later repaid.

sentences.t: Endlich kamen die drei Brüder in ein Schloß, wo in den Ställen lauter steinerne Pferde standen, auch war kein Mensch zu sehen, und sie giengen durch alle Säle, bis sie vor eine Thür ganz am Ende kamen, davor hiengen drei Schlösser;
sentences.l: At last the three brothers came into a castle, where in the stalls stood nothing but stone horses, no person was to be seen either, and they went through all the halls until they came before a door quite at the end, before it hung three locks;
sentences.i: At last the three brothers came to a castle where nothing but stone horses stood in the stables, and not a soul was to be seen; and they went through all the halls until they came to a door right at the end, with three locks hanging on it.
sentences.n: lauter here means “nothing but, sheer,” not “louder.” Schloß is both castle and lock, so the same word stands twice in this sentence in two different senses.

sentences.t: es war aber mitten in der Thüre ein Lädlein, dadurch konnte man in die Stube sehen.
sentences.l: but there was in the middle of the door a little-shutter, through it one could see into the room.
sentences.i: But in the middle of the door there was a little hatch, through which one could see into the room.
sentences.n: Lädlein is a diminutive of Laden, a shutter — the small hinged panel set in an old door for looking through.

sentences.t: Da sahen sie ein graues Männchen, das an einem Tisch saß.
sentences.l: There they saw a little grey man, who sat at a table.
sentences.n: Männchen is a diminutive of Mann, and diminutives are neuter — which is why the tale then calls him es, “it,” all the way through the scene.

sentences.t: Sie riefen es an, einmal, zweimal, aber es hörte nicht: endlich riefen sie zum drittenmal, da stand es auf, öffnete die Schlösser und kam heraus.
sentences.l: They called to it, once, twice, but it did not hear: at last they called for the third time, then it stood up, opened the locks and came out.
sentences.i: They called to him — once, twice — but he did not hear; at last they called a third time, and then he rose, opened the locks and came out.

sentences.t: Er sprach aber kein Wort, sondern führte sie zu einem reichbesetzten Tisch; und als sie gegessen und getrunken hatten, brachte es einen jeglichen in sein eigenes Schlafgemach.
sentences.l: He however spoke no word, but rather led them to a richly-laid table; and when they had eaten and drunk, it brought each one into his own sleeping-chamber.
sentences.i: But he spoke never a word, and led them instead to a richly laid table; and when they had eaten and drunk, he brought each of them to his own bedchamber.
sentences.n: The pronoun changes in mid-sentence — er for the man, then es for the neuter Männchen. The 1857 text does this and we keep it. jeglicher is an old, elevated word for jeder (each).

sentences.t: Am andern Morgen kam das graue Männchen zu dem ältesten, winkte und leitete ihn zu einer steinernen Tafel, darauf standen drei Aufgaben geschrieben, wodurch das Schloß erlöst werden könnte.
sentences.l: On the other morning the grey little-man came to the eldest, beckoned and led him to a stone tablet, upon it stood three tasks written, whereby the castle could be released.
sentences.i: The next morning the little grey man came to the eldest, beckoned, and led him to a stone tablet on which three tasks stood written, by which the castle might be delivered.
sentences.n: “am andern Morgen” = the next morning. Something written “stands” in German where English simply has it written. erlösen is the weighty word Grimm keeps for release from an enchantment.

sentences.t: Die erste war, in dem Wald unter dem Moos lagen die Perlen der Königstochter, tausend an der Zahl, die mußten aufgesucht werden, und wenn vor Sonnenuntergang noch eine einzige fehlte, so ward der, welcher gesucht hatte, zu Stein.
sentences.l: The first was, in the forest under the moss lay the pearls of the king’s-daughter, a thousand in number, those had to be sought out, and if before sunset even a single one was missing, then he who had searched became stone.
sentences.i: The first was this: in the forest, under the moss, lay the king’s daughter’s pearls, a thousand in number; these had to be found, and if a single one were still missing before sunset, then whoever had searched would be turned to stone.
sentences.n: “tausend an der Zahl” = a thousand in number. ward is the old preterite of werden (modern wurde); German states the penalty in the plain past inside the condition, where English needs “would be turned.”

sentences.t: Der älteste gieng hin und suchte den ganzen Tag, als aber der Tag zu Ende war, hatte er erst hundert gefunden;
sentences.l: The eldest went there and searched the whole day, but when the day was at an end, he had found only a hundred;
sentences.i: The eldest went off and searched the whole day; but when the day was over he had found no more than a hundred.
sentences.n: erst here means “only so far” — the point the count has reached and no further, not “first.”

sentences.t: es geschah wie auf der Tafel stand, er ward in Stein verwandelt.
sentences.l: it happened as it stood on the tablet, he was transformed into stone.
sentences.i: It happened as the tablet had said: he was turned to stone.

sentences.t: Am folgenden Tag unternahm der zweite Bruder das Abenteuer: es gieng ihm aber nicht viel besser als dem ältesten, er fand nicht mehr als zweihundert Perlen, und ward zu Stein.
sentences.l: On the following day the second brother undertook the adventure: but it went not much better for him than for the eldest, he found not more than two hundred pearls, and became stone.
sentences.i: The next day the second brother undertook the venture; but he fared little better than the eldest — he found no more than two hundred pearls, and was turned to stone.
sentences.n: “es gieng ihm nicht besser” — German says “it went to him,” putting the person in the dative, where English says “he fared.”

sentences.t: Endlich kam auch an den Dummling die Reihe, der suchte im Moos, es war aber so schwer die Perlen zu finden und gieng so langsam.
sentences.l: At last the turn came also to the Dummling, that one searched in the moss, but it was so hard to find the pearls and went so slowly.
sentences.i: At last it came to be Dummling’s turn; he searched in the moss, but the pearls were so hard to find, and it went so slowly.
sentences.n: “die Reihe kommt an jemanden” = someone’s turn comes. der then opens the next clause as a pointing demonstrative — “that one searched.”

sentences.t: Da setzte er sich auf einen Stein und weinte.
sentences.l: Then he set himself down on a stone and wept.

sentences.t: Und wie er so saß, kam der Ameisenkönig, dem er einmal das Leben erhalten hatte, mit fünftausend Ameisen, und es währte gar nicht lange, so hatten die kleinen Thiere die Perlen mit einander gefunden und auf einen Haufen getragen.
sentences.l: And as he sat so, there came the ant-king, to whom he had once preserved the life, with five thousand ants, and it lasted not long at all, and the little animals had found the pearls among them and carried them onto one heap.
sentences.i: And as he sat there the ant king came, whose life he had once spared, with five thousand ants; and it was no time at all before the little creatures had found the pearls between them and carried them into a single heap.
sentences.n: “jemandem das Leben erhalten” = to preserve someone’s life. “es währte nicht lange, so…” is an old turn of phrase: it did not last long, and then — i.e. before long.

sentences.t: Die zweite Aufgabe aber war, den Schlüssel zu der Schlafkammer der Königstochter aus der See zu holen.
sentences.l: The second task however was, to fetch the key to the sleeping-chamber of the king’s-daughter out of the sea.
sentences.i: The second task was to fetch the key to the king’s daughter’s bedchamber up out of the water.
sentences.n: The water was ein See, masculine, a lake, when the ducks appeared; here it is die See, feminine, which ordinarily means the sea. The text simply wavers, and the ducks are the same ducks — so it is the same water.

sentences.t: Wie der Dummling zur See kam, schwammen die Enten, die er einmal gerettet hatte, heran, tauchten unter, und holten den Schlüssel aus der Tiefe.
sentences.l: When the Dummling came to the water, the ducks, which he had once saved, swam up, dived under, and fetched the key out of the depth.
sentences.i: When Dummling came to the water, the ducks he had once saved swam up, dived under, and brought the key from the deep.

sentences.t: Die dritte Aufgabe aber war die schwerste, aus den drei schlafenden Töchtern des Königs sollte die jüngste und die liebste heraus gesucht werden.
sentences.l: The third task however was the hardest: out of the three sleeping daughters of the king the youngest and the dearest was to be searched out.
sentences.i: But the third task was the hardest: out of the king’s three sleeping daughters, the youngest and dearest had to be picked out.
sentences.n: “heraus gesucht werden” — to be searched out, singled out from among; the 1857 text prints the separable heraus as a word of its own.

sentences.t: Sie glichen sich aber vollkommen, und waren durch nichts verschieden, als daß sie, bevor sie eingeschlafen waren, verschiedene Süßigkeiten gegessen hatten, die älteste ein Stück Zucker, die zweite ein wenig Syrup, die jüngste einen Löffel voll Honig.
sentences.l: But they resembled one another perfectly, and were in nothing different, except that they, before they had fallen asleep, had eaten different sweet things, the eldest a piece of sugar, the second a little syrup, the youngest a spoonful of honey.
sentences.i: But they were perfectly alike, and differed in nothing except that, before falling asleep, they had each eaten something different and sweet — the eldest a lump of sugar, the second a little syrup, the youngest a spoonful of honey.
sentences.n: als here is “except,” not “when” or “as.” Syrup keeps the older spelling (modern Sirup): treacle, thick sugar syrup.

sentences.t: Da kam die Bienenkönigin von den Bienen, die der Dummling vor dem Feuer geschützt hatte, und versuchte den Mund von allen dreien, zuletzt blieb sie auf dem Mund sitzen, der Honig gegessen hatte, und so erkannte der Königssohn die rechte.
sentences.l: Then came the queen of the bees that the Dummling had protected from the fire, and tried the mouth of all three, at last she remained sitting on the mouth that had eaten honey, and so the king’s-son knew the right one.
sentences.i: Then came the queen of the bees Dummling had saved from the fire, and she tried the mouths of all three; at last she settled on the mouth that had eaten honey, and so the king’s son knew the right one.
sentences.n: “sitzen bleiben” = to stay sitting, to settle and not stir. The relative clause “der Honig gegessen hatte” hangs on Mund — grammatically it is the mouth that ate the honey, not the girl.

sentences.t: Da war der Zauber vorbei, alles war aus dem Schlaf erlöst, und wer von Stein war, erhielt seine menschliche Gestalt wieder.
sentences.l: Then the magic was past, everything was released out of the sleep, and whoever was of stone received his human shape again.
sentences.i: Then the enchantment was over, all was released from its sleep, and whoever was of stone received his human shape again.

sentences.t: Und der Dummling vermählte sich mit der jüngsten und liebsten, und ward König nach ihres Vaters Tod; seine zwei Brüder aber erhielten die beiden andern Schwestern.
sentences.l: And the Dummling married himself to the youngest and dearest, and became king after her father’s death; his two brothers however received the two other sisters.
sentences.i: And Dummling wedded the youngest and dearest, and became king after her father’s death; but his two brothers had the other two sisters.
sentences.n: “sich vermählen mit” is the elevated word for marrying. “nach ihres Vaters Tod” sets the genitive before its noun, an old and formal order. The two mockers are not punished; they are simply married to the sisters left over.
